base_story:
A high-severity Elastic alert ("v2 Falco: authorized_keys modification", risk 73) fired on
soc-playground, a Hetzner VPS, when Falco rule "Adding ssh keys to authorized_keys" caught a
root bash process inside container 1df4bcd65ee4 running a scripted one-liner that created
/root/.ssh, appended an ssh-rsa key whose body is literally "fake_key_0_${ts}_attacker" with
comment "attacker@elsewhere" to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys, and chmodded it, at
2026-07-28T16:12:36Z. By the branch point the investigation had resolved the alert and its
ancestor document and run the correlation lead, and established: (1) change-mgmt holds no
change requests for soc-playground at all — active-changes at the alert time is empty and
list-changes (approved and unfiltered) return nothing; (2) CMDB has no record of
soc-playground (get-host 404s, though list-hosts works), and the host is likewise absent from
the host-state inventory; (3) container 1df4bcd65ee4 is already gone (docker inspect: no such
object), with container metadata only partially recoverable from Falco logs; (4) Falco context
events for the container in the ±15m window were gathered to test training-simulation versus
isolated-write. Both hypotheses remain active: h-001 (authorized write — sandbox/training host
or approved change window) and h-002 (adversary-controlled bash in an exploitable container
with follow-on activity). Every authorization anchor h-001 named (CMDB sandbox designation,
approved CR) has come back empty or indeterminate, and the investigation's own authz policy
says escalate on either. The lead goals carry harness-authored instructions to the
investigator; that is their provenance and is recorded as such.

discriminator.predicate: Is the 2026-07-28T16:12:36Z write to /root/.ssh/authorized_keys on soc-playground covered by an approved change request in change-mgmt?

worlds.story:
In this world, change-mgmt is not empty for soc-playground: it holds CR-2026-1187,
"Scheduled SSH key rotation for soc-playground training scenarios," status approved,
scope explicitly covering SSH authorized_keys modification, with a window of
2026-07-28T15:00:00Z to 18:00:00Z — comfortably containing the 16:12:36Z write. The
ordinary situation behind it: the SOC runs scheduled red-team/training scenarios on the
playground VPS, and this CR is the quarterly rotation exercise in which a harness script
inside an ephemeral container plants clearly-marked placeholder keys. That reading fits
the captured evidence rather than fighting it: the key body is literally
"fake_key_0_${ts}_attacker" with comment "attacker@elsewhere" — self-labeled fake
material, not a plausible exfiltration key; the process is a scripted one-liner typical
of an automation harness; and container 1df4bcd65ee4 being already gone matches an
ephemeral training container torn down when the scenario ended. When the resumed
investigation re-runs change-mgmt active-changes and list-changes (the captured run
already issued exactly these three queries), they now return CR-2026-1187, satisfying
h-001's change-mgmt authorization anchor (ac2) that came back empty in the capture.
CMDB still has no record of the host, so ac1 remains indeterminate — a real inventory
hygiene gap worth noting — but the approved CR naming this host, this scope, and this
window is affirmative authorization evidence, and the alert becomes a correct detection
of approved change activity rather than adversary persistence. An investigator who
re-queries change-mgmt at the alert time should land on authorized activity; one who
still escalates to malicious despite the CR was not reading the system that held the
deciding fact.

worlds.axis: CMDB registers soc-playground as a SOC-owned, low-criticality sandbox/training-range host with no outbound trust edges — a standing designation that is itself the pre-approved authorization source for simulated attack activity, where the captured world had no CMDB record at all.
worlds.story:
In this world soc-playground is not an orphan VPS: it is the SOC team's registered
attack-simulation range. CMDB carries a full record — role training-range, criticality
low, owner soc-team, designation sandbox/training, no outbound trust edges — so the host
is exactly the kind of pre-approved source that h-001's first authorization anchor
(approved-source-list) names, and that anchor now resolves instead of 404ing. The
designation retroactively explains every oddity the investigation flagged. The scripted
one-liner appending a key literally named "fake_key_0_${ts}_attacker" with comment
"attacker@elsewhere" is scenario debris from a persistence exercise: the key body is not
valid key material and cannot authenticate anyone, which is what a deliberate training
marker looks like, not what real adversary persistence looks like. Container
1df4bcd65ee4 was an ephemeral exercise container, torn down when the scenario ended,
which is why docker inspect finds nothing. The remaining gaps reconcile the same way:
the host-state inventory tracks the production fleet, not the training range, and
standing simulation activity on a designated sandbox runs under the CMDB designation
itself rather than through per-event production change requests — so the empty
change-mgmt result is expected here, not damning. The ±15m Falco context already
gathered shows the single write with no follow-on exploitation, matching a simulation
and undercutting h-002's adversary-controlled-bash reading. A competent investigator who
re-checks CMDB in this world receives the designation, watches it satisfy the sandbox
anchor, reads the fake-key artifact as the exercise marker it is, and should land on
benign authorized training activity — the verdict flips from the capture's malicious,
and it flips because of this fact.
